questions.question: Q: What percentage of the GCSE grade is NEA Task 1 worth (AQA)?

points.text: 15% of the total GCSE grade. It is completed in controlled conditions over approximately 10 hours.

questions.question: Q: What is the purpose of NEA Task 1?

points.text: To assess students' understanding of the working characteristics, functional properties, and chemical processes of ingredients through a scientific investigation.

questions.question: Q: What is a controlled variable and why is it important in a food investigation?

points.text: A controlled variable is a factor kept constant during experiments (e.g. oven temperature, ingredient quantities, cooking time). It is essential so that any differences in results can be attributed to the independent variable being tested, not other factors.

questions.question: Q: What should a food investigation report include?

points.text: Research, hypothesis, method (including controlled variables), results table, sensory evaluation, photographic evidence, analysis linked to food science, conclusion, and practical applications.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between the independent variable and the dependent variable?

points.text: The independent variable is the factor you change (e.g. type of raising agent). The dependent variable is the outcome you measure (e.g. cake volume, texture).

questions.question: Q: Why is sensory evaluation used in food investigations?

points.text: To objectively compare the taste, texture, appearance, and aroma of test products using rating scales (e.g. 1–5), providing evidence beyond just visual or quantitative data.

questions.question: Q: Give an example of a suitable Task 1 investigation brief.

points.text: 'Investigate how different types of fat (butter, margarine, and vegetable oil) affect the shortness and texture of shortcrust pastry.' or 'Investigate the effect of different raising agents on the volume of a sponge cake.'

questions.question: Q: Why must the conclusion link to food science?

points.text: Because Task 1 assesses understanding of functional properties and chemical processes. The conclusion must explain WHY results occurred using scientific knowledge (e.g. 'butter produced shorter pastry because its fat coats flour proteins, preventing gluten formation').

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: I would investigate how three raising agents — baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, and self-raising flour — affect sponge cake volume and texture. The independent variable is the type of raising agent. The dependent variables are cake volume (measured in cm³ by displacement or height) and texture (assessed by sensory evaluation). Controlled variables include: 50g each of flour, sugar, butter, and one egg; oven temperature 180°C; baking time 20 minutes; same mixing method (creaming); same cake tin size and material; same cooling time before measurement. I would make three cakes, changing only the raising agent: Cake A uses baking powder (1 teaspoon), Cake B uses bicarbonate of soda (half teaspoon, with an acidic ingredient like lemon juice), Cake C uses self-raising flour (replacing plain flour). After baking and cooling, I would measure the height and volume of each cake, photograph cross-sections, and conduct a sensory evaluation with at least three testers rating texture, lightness, and overall acceptability on a 1–5 scale. Results would be recorded in a table comparing raising agent, height, volume, and sensory scores. I would repeat the experiment once to verify reliability. In my analysis, I would link results to food science: baking powder contains both an alkali and acid that react with moisture and heat to produce CO2; bicarbonate of soda requires an external acid to react; self-raising flour contains a measured amount of baking powder.
